alignment.note: Greek ἐπετίμησεν is a single aorist verb; the Vulgate renders the idea periphrastically with the perfect deponent comminatus est, while the Peshitta ܘܟܐܐ (root k-a, 'to rebuke') fuses the conjunction and verb into one form, hence its overlap with the preceding καί group.

Greek carries the articular subject ὁ Ἰησοῦς; both Syriac and Latin omit the definite article since neither language possesses a formal counterpart to the Greek article, rendering simply ܝܫܘܥ / Jesus.

Greek λέγων is a present participle subordinating the speech; the Peshitta ܘܐܡܪ uses a finite verb with conjunctive waw ('and he said'), a typical Semitic paratactic construction, while the Vulgate retains the participle dicens followed by a colon marking direct discourse.

Greek φιμώθητι ('be muzzled/silenced') is a single passive imperative; the Peshitta expands idiomatically to ܣܟܘܪ ܦܘܡܟ ('shut your mouth'), making the implied organ explicit, whereas the Vulgate Obmutesce ('become dumb') matches the Greek with one verb.

The Peshitta ܘܦܘܩ fuses conjunction and imperative ('and come out') into a single form, hence its index overlaps with the preceding καί group, while Greek ἔξελθε and Latin exi stand as discrete imperatives.

Greek ἐξ αὐτοῦ and Syriac ܡܢܗ use the bare pronoun ('out of him'); the Vulgate substitutes the explicit noun de homine ('out of the man'), an interpretive expansion clarifying the antecedent that is absent from both the Greek and Syriac witnesses.
